newsitem.title: UK: Wounded man arrested after Northern Ireland blast.
newsitem.headline: Wounded man arrested after Northern Ireland blast.

text.p: A 19-year-old man who was shot and seriously wounded after a suspected bomb attack on a police station in rural Northern Ireland was under arrest in his hospital bed on Thursday, a police source said.
"A person has been arrested. He is under armed guard," the source said.
The man was shot in the stomach at Coalisland, County Tyrone, in what appeared to have been an undercover operation mounted by British troops.
The shooting happened around the time of an explosion which local people had said they thought had been caused by a "stun grenade" being fired by security forces.

But police sources said a hole had been found in the perimeter fence at the town's Royal Ulster Constabulary station and it was probably caused by "an explosive device containing at least one kilo of high explosives."
The wounded man underwent emergency surgery for a stomach wound, said Robert Sowney, a spokesman for South Tyrone Hospital. "His condition is ill but stable," he told Reuters.
Two people arrested in a follow-up operation were still being questioned on Thursday afternoon, according to security sources.
Several homes were evacuated in a housing estate behind the police station and a British army bomb disposal officer had been called to the scene in the early hours of the morning.

The incidents coincided with heightened tension in the province where Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas have launched a series of attacks on British security forces and a truce by pro-British Loyalist extremists is fragile.
The IRA, which is fighting to end British rule, is suspected of carrying out two bomb attacks that disrupted rail services in northwestern England on Thursday.
Despite the bombs, Irish security sources do not rule out a fresh IRA truce, an Irish newspaper said Thursday.
"Security sources hopeful of new IRA ceasefire," the Irish Times newspaper said above a front-page article.

The paper said political activists had regained lost ground within the so-called Republican Movement, which embraces the IRA and its Sinn Fein political arm, and that guerrillas might move to get Sinn Fein into talks with Britain.
Britain says the IRA must abandon violence for Sinn Fein to gain entry to talks.
